module_title: The Revolt of 1857 - Causes, Centers, and Failure
introduction: At this level, we look beyond the greased cartridges to the deep-rooted political and administrative causes. We will also study the regional leaders, the British officers who suppressed them, and the reasons why the revolt ultimately failed.

core_concepts.title: Political Causes
core_concepts.description: Lord Dalhousie's 'Doctrine of Lapse' (annexing Jhansi, Satara, etc. for lacking a natural heir) and the annexation of Awadh (1856) on charges of 'misgovernance' created massive political unrest.

core_concepts.title: Major Centers and Leaders
core_concepts.description: The revolt was led by Nana Saheb in Kanpur (assisted by Tatya Tope), Begum Hazrat Mahal in Lucknow, Rani Lakshmibai in Jhansi, and Kunwar Singh in Bihar (Jagdishpur).

core_concepts.title: British Suppressors
core_concepts.description: The revolt was ruthlessly crushed by British officers: John Nicholson and Hudson in Delhi, Colin Campbell in Kanpur and Lucknow, and General Hugh Rose in Jhansi.

core_concepts.title: Reasons for Failure
core_concepts.description: The uprising failed due to a lack of unified command and central leadership, limited territorial spread (confined mostly to North and Central India), and lack of modern weapons compared to the British.

core_concepts.title: Classes that Stayed Aloof
core_concepts.description: The Western-educated Indians, modern zamindars, and many princely states (like Scindia of Gwalior and Holkar of Indore) did not join the revolt; some even actively helped the British.

important_entities.name: Tatya Tope
important_entities.significance: His real name was Ramachandra Pandurang. He used brilliant guerrilla warfare tactics against the British for a long time.

important_entities.name: Kunwar Singh
important_entities.significance: An 80-year-old Zamindar of Jagdishpur (Arrah) who provided outstanding leadership in Bihar and defeated British forces multiple times.

important_entities.name: General Hugh Rose
important_entities.significance: He defeated Rani Lakshmibai and famously remarked about her: 'Here lay the woman who was the only man among the rebels'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Never assume the revolt covered the whole country. South India (Madras presidency), large parts of Punjab, and western India remained largely undisturbed.
A common misconception is that all Indians supported the mutiny. The educated Indian middle class actually opposed it, believing that British rule would help modernize India.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: A quick associative link: Kanpur-Nana, Lucknow-Begum Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi-Rani, Bihar-Kunwar.

exam_strategy_tips: 'Match the following' questions pairing the Center, the Indian Leader, and the British Suppressing Officer are highly probable.
Remember the chronological order of states annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Baghat, Udaipur, Jhansi, Nagpur).
